Knee Push-Up: Kneel with hands under your shoulders and a straight line from head to knees. Lower your chest to the floor with elbows at a slight angle, then push back up. Letting the hips sag turns it into a poor plank.
L-Sit Pull-Up: Hang from the bar with legs lifted in front, toes pointed, holding an L shape. Pull your chin over the bar while keeping the legs raised, then lower with control. Dropping the legs midway loses the position fastest.
Long-Lever Plank: Set up in a forearm plank but walk your elbows further out in front of your shoulders. Brace your abs and hold a straight line from head to heels. Letting the hips drop removes most of the challenge.
Marching Glute Bridge (Alternating): Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat, then lift your hips into a bridge. Keeping the hips level, raise one knee towards your chest and swap sides while staying lifted. Letting the raised hip drop is the main fault.
Mixed Grip Pull-Up: Hang from the bar with one palm facing you and the other facing away. Pull yourself up until your chin clears the bar, then lower under control. Swap grip sides evenly rather than always leading with the same hand.
Muscle-Up (Bar): Hang from the bar with active shoulders, then pull explosively while leaning forward over it. Roll your wrists over as your chest clears the bar and press out to lock your arms. Slowing down mid-pull tends to strand you under the bar.
Neck Bridge (Front): Kneel and rest your forehead on a soft mat, walking your feet back until weight sits gently on your head and hands. Rock forward and back through a small range while your neck supports the load. Rushing the range is the common error.
Negative Pull-Up (Eccentric-Only): Jump or step up so your chin is above the bar, then lower yourself as slowly as you can manage. Keep your shoulders engaged rather than letting your body drop loosely. Rushing the lowering phase defeats the point of the drill.
Parallette Push-Up (Deep Range): Grip the parallettes with hands under your shoulders, body in a straight line. Lower your chest below hand height for a deeper range than the floor allows, then press back up. Flaring the elbows wide at the bottom loses chest tension.
Pike Push-Up: Start in a pike position, hips high, hands and feet on the floor forming an inverted V. Bend your elbows to lower the top of your head towards the floor, then press back up. Letting the hips drop turns this into a regular push-up.
Pistol Squat: Stand on one leg with the other reaching out in front, arms forward for balance. Bend the standing knee to lower until your hip nears your heel, then drive back up. Letting the knee cave inward is the common breakdown under fatigue.
Planche Lean: Get into a push-up position and shift your shoulders forward over your hands, arms staying straight. Hold the lean at the point where your heels just lift, then return. Bending the elbows to compensate removes the point of the drill.
Plank Shoulder Tap: Hold a high plank with hands under your shoulders and feet set wide for stability. Tap one shoulder with the opposite hand while keeping your hips still, then alternate. Rocking the hips side to side means the core is coasting.
Plank to Push-Up (Walk-Up): Start in a forearm plank, then press up onto one hand at a time until you reach a high plank, and reverse the sequence. Keep your hips steady throughout. Letting the hips twist or sag gives away the point of the drill.
Pseudo-Planche Push-Up: Set up in a push-up position, hands turned slightly inward and set further back near your hips. Lean your shoulders forward past your hands as you lower, then press back up. Hands drifting forward turns it back into a normal push-up.
RKC Plank: Hold a forearm plank while actively squeezing your glutes and pulling your elbows towards your toes without moving them. Brace hard for a shorter hold than a standard plank. Relaxing the squeeze partway through loses most of the benefit.
Scapular Pull-Up: Hang from the bar with straight arms and relaxed shoulders. Without bending your elbows, pull your shoulder blades down and together to lift a small amount, then release. Bending the arms turns this into a small pull-up.
Scapular Push-Up: Start in a push-up position with straight arms. Let your shoulder blades pinch together to lower your chest slightly, then push the floor away to round your upper back. Bending the elbows takes the movement away from the shoulder blades.
Scissor Kick: Lie on your back with legs straight, lifted a little off the floor, hands under your lower back for support. Cross one leg over the other, alternating which leg is on top. Letting your lower back arch off the floor loses abs tension.
Shrimp Squat: Stand on one leg holding the other foot behind you with the same-side hand. Bend the standing knee to lower until the back knee nearly touches the floor, then stand back up. Pitching the torso too far forward makes the balance far harder.
Side Plank with Hip Dip (Dynamic): Prop yourself on one forearm in a side plank, feet stacked. Lower your hip towards the floor and lift it back to the start line, keeping the movement small and controlled. Twisting the torso forward turns this into a rock, not a hip dip.
Single-Arm Inverted Row: Lie under a bar set at hip height and grip it with one hand, body straight from head to heels. Pull your chest towards the bar while keeping your body rigid, then lower under control. Letting the hips sag shifts the load away from the back.
Single-Leg Glute Bridge: Lie on your back with one knee bent and foot flat, the other leg extended straight or held to the chest. Drive through the planted heel to lift your hips, squeezing the glute at the top. Letting the hips tilt to one side is the main fault.
Spiderman Push-Up: Start in a push-up position and, as you lower your chest, bring one knee towards the same-side elbow. Return the leg as you press back up, then alternate sides. Barely bringing the knee to the elbow undoes the point of the drive.
Stability Ball Knee Tuck: Place your shins on a stability ball in a push-up position, hands under your shoulders. Roll the ball towards you by drawing your knees to your chest, then extend back out. Hips piking up too early takes the challenge off the core.
Staggered Hands Push-Up: Get into a push-up position with one hand set further forward than the other. Lower your chest towards the floor and press back up, keeping the stagger throughout. Letting the hips rotate towards the back hand is the common fault.
Straight Bar Dip (Chest-Lean): Grip a straight bar and support yourself with arms locked, leaning your torso forward from the shoulders. Bend your elbows to lower your chest towards the bar, then press back up. Staying upright shifts the emphasis away from the chest.
Tuck Jump: Stand with feet hip-width apart and knees soft. Jump straight up and drive both knees towards your chest at the top, then land softly with bent knees. Landing with straight, locked knees is the biggest thing to correct.
Tuck Planche Hold: Sit tall with hands beside your hips and knees drawn tightly to your chest. Press down through your hands to lift your whole body off the floor, arms staying straight. Hips drifting behind your shoulders makes the hold much harder.
Typewriter Pull-Up: Pull yourself up until your chin is above the bar, then shift sideways towards one hand while staying up, and back across to the other. Keep your chin above the bar throughout. Dropping down between sides splits it into two pull-ups.
Typewriter Push-Up: Lower into a wide push-up until your chest nears the floor, then shift sideways towards one bent arm while the other stays straight. Slide back across before pressing up. Letting the chest rise during the shift undoes the drill.
V-Sit: Sit on the floor and lean back slightly, lifting your legs straight so your body forms a V with your torso. Hold the position with arms reaching forward or resting beside you. Rounding through the lower back is the usual compensation.
Wall Handstand Hold: Kick up into a handstand facing a wall, walking your hands back until upright and braced against it. Press firmly through your hands and hold the position steady. Letting the lower back arch heavily is the most common thing to tidy up.
Wall Handstand Push-Up: Set up in a wall handstand, hands slightly wider than shoulder width. Bend your elbows to lower the top of your head towards the floor, then press back to full lock out. Flaring the elbows wide takes work away from the shoulders.
Weighted Chin-Up: Hang from the bar with palms facing you and a weight at your waist or between your feet. Pull your chin above the bar leading with your chest, then lower fully under control. Rushing the lowering under the extra load is the main fault.
Windshield Wiper (Hanging): Hang from the bar and raise your straight legs to hip height in front of you. Rotate your legs together side to side like a windscreen wiper, keeping your shoulders stable. Swinging from momentum rather than the abs is the main fault.
Seated Band Lat Pulldown: Sit tall with the band anchored overhead, gripped wide in both hands. Pull it down towards your upper chest by driving your elbows down and back, then let it return with control. Leaning back to use bodyweight is the common shortcut.
Seated Band Row: Sit with legs extended and the band looped around your feet, an end in each hand. Pull your elbows back past your ribs while keeping your chest tall, then extend forward. Rounding the back to add range loses tension in the target muscles.
Band Ankle Dorsiflexion: Sit with the band looped around the top of one foot, anchored in front of you. Pull your toes up towards your shin against the band, then release slowly. Using the whole leg to yank the band cuts the ankle out of it.
Band Ankle Plantarflexion: Sit with legs extended, the band looped around the ball of one foot, held taut in your hands. Point your toes away from you against the band, then return with control. Bending the knee to help the push takes work off the calf.
Band Assisted Ab Wheel Rollout: Kneel and loop a band over a high anchor and around the ab wheel to reduce the load. Roll the wheel forward keeping hips level and back flat, then pull back to kneeling. Letting the hips sag towards the floor is the main fault.
Band Assisted Dip: Loop a band around the dip bars and place a knee or foot in the loop for support. Lower your body by bending your elbows, then press back up to full lock out. Leaning too far forward shifts work from triceps towards the chest.
Band Chest Fly (Standing): Anchor the band behind you at chest height, an end in each hand, arms out to the sides with a slight elbow bend. Bring your hands together in front of your chest in a wide arc, then return slowly. More elbow bend turns it into a press.
Band Chest Press (Single-Arm): Anchor the band behind you at chest height, standing in a staggered stance holding one end at chest level. Press your hand forward until the arm is straight, then return with control. Twisting the torso to help takes work off the chest.
Band Clamshell: Lie on your side with knees bent and a band looped around your thighs, feet stacked together. Keeping your feet touching, lift your top knee towards the ceiling, then lower it back. Rolling your hips backward loses the position fastest.
Band Concentration Curl: Sit with the band anchored under your foot, elbow braced against the inside of your thigh. Curl your hand up towards your shoulder, then lower fully under control. Letting the elbow drift off the thigh brings the shoulder into the lift.
Band Fire Hydrant (Kneeling): Kneel on all fours with a band looped around your thighs just above the knees. Lift one knee out to the side keeping your hips square, then lower it back. Letting the hips rotate open is the main compensation to watch.
Band Front Raise: Stand on the band, feet hip-width apart, an end in each hand in front of your thighs. Raise your arms straight in front to shoulder height, then lower with control. Swinging from the hips to launch the band takes work off the shoulders.
Band Glute Bridge: Lie on your back with knees bent and a band looped around your thighs, feet flat on the floor. Drive your hips up while pressing your knees out against the band, squeezing at the top. Knees collapsing inward is the fault to expose.
Band Glute Kickback: Get on all fours with the band looped around one foot, anchored under the other knee or a fixed point. Extend the banded leg straight back and up without arching your back, then return. Arching the spine for height loses glute work.
Band Goblet Squat: Stand on the centre of the band, feet shoulder-width apart, both ends held at chest height like a goblet. Sit your hips back and down into a squat, chest tall, then drive back up. The band pulling your shoulders forward rounds the back.
Band Hammer Curl: Stand on the band, feet hip-width apart, an end in each hand with palms facing your body. Curl your hands up towards your shoulders keeping your palms in, then lower fully. Swinging the elbows forward turns the curl into a shoulder move.
Band Hip Thrust (Single-Leg): Sit with your upper back against a bench, a band anchored low behind you and looped around your hips. Drive through one heel to lift your hips, other leg lifted, then lower with control. Twisting towards the working leg is the common fault.
Band Incline Press: Anchor the band low behind you, an end in each hand at shoulder height, staggered stance leaning slightly forward. Press your hands up and forward at an incline angle, then return slowly. Arching the back for range takes work off the chest.
Band Leg Extension: Sit tall with the band anchored behind you and looped around one ankle. Extend that knee straight out in front against the band, then lower with control. Leaning back to use momentum takes the work away from the quad.
Band Monster Walk: Loop a band around your thighs or ankles and drop into a quarter squat, knees pressed slightly out. Step sideways in small steps keeping tension on the band, then repeat the other way. Letting the knees drift inward loses the point of it.
Band Pallof Press: Stand side on to the anchor with the band at chest height, both hands together in front of your sternum. Press your hands out away from your chest without rotating the torso towards the anchor, then return. Twisting is what it resists.
Band Pull-Apart (Overhead): Hold the band overhead, hands wider than shoulder width, arms straight. Pull the band apart by driving your hands out and slightly down, squeezing your shoulder blades, then return. Bending the elbows turns it into a pulldown.
Band Rear Delt Fly: Anchor the band in front of you at chest height, an end in each hand, arms extended. Pull your hands out and back in a wide arc, squeezing your shoulder blades, then return slowly. Bending the elbows too much shifts the work elsewhere.
Band Romanian Deadlift (Bilateral): Stand on the band, feet hip-width apart, an end in each hand in front of your thighs. Push your hips back and lower the band down your legs with a soft knee bend, then drive forward to stand. Rounding the lower back is the main fault.
Band Romanian Deadlift (Single-Leg): Stand on the band with one foot, an end in each hand, weight shifted onto that leg. Hinge forward at the hip while the other leg extends back for balance, then return to standing. Letting the hips rotate open signals losing control.
Band Row (Single-Arm): Anchor the band at chest height and stand side on, holding one end in a staggered stance. Pull your elbow back past your ribs keeping your torso still, then extend forward. Rotating the torso to help takes tension off the back.
Band Seated Row: Sit on the floor with legs extended, the band anchored at foot height, an end in each hand. Pull your elbows straight back close to your ribs, squeezing the shoulder blades, then extend forward. Leaning back loses mid-back tension.
Band Shoulder Press (Seated): Sit tall on a chair or bench, band anchored under the seat, an end in each hand at shoulder height. Press hands straight overhead, then lower back to shoulder height. Arching the back for height takes work off the shoulders.
Band Standing Curl (Single-Arm): Stand on the band with one foot, holding the free end in the same-side hand, arm extended. Curl your hand up towards your shoulder without swinging the elbow forward, then lower fully. Leaning back shifts work away from the biceps.
Band Standing Hip Abduction: Stand side on to the anchor, band around your ankle, a wall or support nearby for balance. Lift the banded leg straight out to the side without leaning your torso, then lower with control. Leaning away lets momentum do the work.
Band Standing Hip Adduction: Stand side on to the anchor, band around your ankle, anchor on the same side as the working leg. Pull the leg across your body towards the midline, then return under control. Rotating the hips to help takes tension off the inner thigh.
Band Straight-Arm Pulldown: Stand facing a high anchor, holding the band with arms extended in front at shoulder height. Pull your hands down towards your thighs keeping your elbows straight, then let it return slowly. Bending the elbows turns it into a pushdown.
Band Sumo Deadlift: Stand on the band, feet wide and toes turned out, an end in each hand between your legs. Push your hips back and bend your knees into the wide stance, then drive through your heels to stand tall. Knees caving inward is the fault.
Band T-Raise: Hinge forward with a flat back, band anchored in front of you, an end in each hand. Raise your arms out to the sides until level with your shoulders, forming a T, then lower with control. Heaving with the back takes work off the shoulders.
Band Tricep Kickback: Hinge forward with a flat back, upper arm close to your body and elbow bent, band anchored behind you. Straighten your elbow to extend your hand back, then return under control. Swinging the upper arm turns it into a shoulder movement.
Band Upright Row: Stand on the band, feet hip-width apart, an end in each hand in front of your thighs. Pull your hands up towards your collarbone leading with your elbows, then lower with control. Shrugging up for height takes work off the target muscles.
Band W-Raise: Stand on the band, an end in each hand at your sides. Pull your hands up and out into a W shape by bending your elbows and squeezing your shoulder blades, then return. Dropping the elbows below shoulder height turns the W into a shrug.
Band Woodchop (High-to-Low): Anchor the band up high and stand side on, both hands together near the anchor. Pull the band down and across your body towards your opposite hip, rotating through the torso, then return slowly. Moving only the arms skips the core.
Band Woodchop (Low-to-High): Anchor the band down low and stand side on, both hands together near the anchor. Pull the band up and across your body towards the opposite shoulder, rotating through the torso, then return slowly. Arms alone leave the core out of it.
Band Y-Raise: Stand on the band, feet hip-width apart, an end in each hand in front of your thighs. Raise your arms up and out into a Y shape above your head, then lower with control. Arching the lower back for height takes work off the shoulders.
Band Y-T-W Raise: Stand on the band or anchor it in front of you, an end in each hand. Move through a Y, then a T, then a W shape, keeping your torso still throughout. Using momentum to swing through each position takes the work off the shoulders and back.
Push-Up (Band-Resisted): Loop a band across your upper back and under your hands in a push-up position. Lower your chest to the floor as normal, then press up hard against the extra tension near the top. Letting the band pull your shoulders forward rounds the back.
Archer Row on Rings: Hold two rings at chest height, arms extended, feet set for a moderate lean back. Pull one arm in to row while the other stays straight and reaches towards that ring, then swap sides. A bending straight arm defeats the archer pattern.
Ring Chin-Up: Hang from two rings with palms facing you, arms fully extended. Pull your chin above the rings, letting your hands rotate naturally as you rise, then lower fully under control. Letting the rings swing wildly loses pull stability.
Ring Dip: Hold two rings at your sides, arms locked, palms turned slightly inward. Bend your elbows to lower your body keeping the rings close to your ribs, then press back up to lock out. Letting the rings drift away makes the shoulders unstable.
Ring Fly: Hold two rings with arms extended out to the sides, leaning forward from a supported position. Bring your hands together in front of your chest by bending slightly at the elbows, then return wide. Bending too much turns it into a press.
Ring Muscle-Up: Hang from two rings and pull explosively while leaning your body forward, turning your wrists over as your chest clears the rings. Press through to full lock out. Pulling straight up instead of forward leaves you stuck at chest height.
Ring Pull-Up: Hang from two rings, palms facing away from you, arms fully extended. Pull your chin above the rings, letting your hands rotate as they meet your chest, then lower under control. Rings drifting apart at the top loses shoulder tension.
Ring Support Hold: Push up to full lock out on two rings, arms straight, rings turned out slightly at your sides. Hold your body steady, shoulders pulled down away from your ears. Rings drifting apart or shoulders creeping up is the main thing to correct.
Skin the Cat: Hang from two rings or a bar with straight arms. Tuck your knees and roll your hips up and over so your feet pass below your hands, ending upside down, then reverse back to the start. Rushing the reversal without control is the fault.
TRX Assisted Pistol Squat: Hold the TRX handles at chest height, standing on one leg with the other extended in front. Bend the standing knee into a single-leg squat, using the straps for balance rather than pulling yourself up. Relying on your arms costs leg work.
TRX Assisted Squat: Hold the TRX handles at chest height with straps taut, feet shoulder-width apart. Sit your hips back and down into a squat, using the straps only for balance, then drive back up. Pulling hard on the straps takes load off the legs.
TRX Atomic Push-Up: Place your feet in the TRX foot cradles, hold a push-up position with hands under your shoulders. Lower into a push-up, then draw your knees towards your chest before extending back out. Letting the hips sag breaks the plank position.
TRX Bicep Curl (Single-Arm): Hold one TRX handle and lean back with your arm extended, feet set for a stable base. Curl your hand towards your shoulder by bending the elbow, then extend back out while leaning away. Shoulder drifting forward turns the curl into a row.
TRX Chest Fly: Hold the TRX handles with arms extended out to the sides, leaning forward from a stable stance. Bring your hands together in front of your chest in a wide arc, then return wide. Bending the elbows more each rep turns the fly into a press.
TRX Chest Press: Hold the TRX handles at chest height, leaning forward with your body straight from head to heels. Bend your elbows to lower your chest towards your hands, then press back to the start. Letting the hips sag shifts tension to the lower back.
TRX Chest Press (Single-Arm): Hold one TRX handle at chest height, body straight and leaning forward, other hand free or on your hip. Bend the elbow to lower your chest towards your hand, then press back out. Rotating the torso turns the press into a twist.
TRX Face Pull: Hold the TRX handles with arms extended, leaning back with your body straight. Pull your hands towards your face, driving your elbows out wide and back, then extend back out. Letting the elbows drop low turns the face pull into a row.
TRX Fallout (Rollout): Hold the TRX handles at chest height, kneeling with your body straight. Extend your arms forward and let your body lean out and down as far as you can control, then pull back to the start. Letting the lower back sag is the main fault.
TRX Hamstring Curl: Lie on your back with heels in the TRX foot cradles, hips lifted off the floor. Bend your knees to pull your heels towards your glutes, hips staying raised, then extend back out. Letting the hips drop takes tension off the hamstrings.
TRX Hip Press: Lie on your back with heels in the TRX foot cradles, knees bent. Drive your heels down to lift your hips into a bridge, squeezing your glutes at the top, then lower with control. Letting the hips sag to one side is the common fault.
TRX I-Raise: Hold the TRX handles with arms extended, leaning back with your body straight. Raise your arms straight overhead into an I shape, close to your ears, then lower back down. Bending the elbows takes the work off the shoulders.
TRX Knee Tuck: Place your feet in the TRX foot cradles, hold a plank position with hands under your shoulders. Draw both knees towards your chest, then extend your legs back out. Letting the hips rise during the tuck cuts the core work short.
TRX Mountain Climber (Feet Suspended): Place your feet in the TRX foot cradles, hold a plank with hands under your shoulders. Drive one knee towards your chest then the other in a running motion, hips staying level. Letting the hips bounce up and down is the main fault.
TRX Pike: Place your feet in the TRX foot cradles, hold a plank with hands under your shoulders. Lift your hips towards the ceiling by drawing your legs towards your hands, then return to plank. Bending the knees takes work off the core.
TRX Plank (Feet Suspended): Place your feet in the TRX foot cradles, hold a straight line from head to heels with hands under your shoulders. Brace your core and hold the position steady. Letting the hips sag or pike up is the main thing to correct.
TRX Push-Up (Feet Suspended): Place your feet in the TRX foot cradles, hold a push-up position with hands on the floor under your shoulders. Lower your chest down, then press back up keeping your body straight. Letting the hips sag makes the straps swing.
TRX Rear-Foot Elevated Lunge: Stand facing away from the anchor, one foot in the TRX foot cradle behind you, the other planted forward. Bend both knees to lower into a lunge, then drive through the front foot to stand. The front knee drifting forward loses balance.
TRX Reverse Fly: Hold the TRX handles with arms extended, leaning back with your body straight. Pull your hands out and back into a wide fly, squeezing your shoulder blades together, then return. Bending the elbows too much turns the fly into a row.
TRX Row (Feet Elevated): Place your feet on an elevated surface, hold the TRX handles with your body straight, leaning back further than a standard row. Pull your chest towards your hands, then extend back out. Letting the hips sag shifts tension to the lower back.
TRX Row (Single-Arm): Hold one TRX handle and lean back with your body straight, other hand free or on your hip. Pull your chest towards your hand, then extend back out. Rotating the torso towards the working side turns the row into a twist.
TRX T-Raise: Hold the TRX handles with arms extended, leaning back with your body straight. Raise your arms out to the sides until they form a T, then lower back down. Bending the elbows takes the work away from the shoulders.
TRX Triceps Extension: Hold the TRX handles above your head, leaning forward with your body straight, elbows pointing forward. Bend your elbows to lower your head towards your hands, then extend back straight. Flaring the elbows out shifts work off the triceps.
TRX W-Raise: Hold the TRX handles with arms extended, leaning back with your body straight. Pull your hands up into a W shape by bending your elbows and squeezing your shoulder blades, then return. Dropping the elbows low turns the W into a shrug.
TRX Y-Raise: Hold the TRX handles with arms extended, leaning back with your body straight. Raise your arms up and out into a Y shape above your head, then lower back down. Bending the elbows takes the work away from the shoulders.
Alternating Kettlebell Snatch: Hike the bell back between your legs, then drive your hips forward hard to send it up, punching your hand through at the top. Catch it softly with a straight arm overhead, then lower and swap hands. Muscling it up with the arm wastes power.
Bottoms-Up Kettlebell Carry: Clean the bell to your shoulder and flip it so the base points up, resting in your palm with a tight grip. Walk forward keeping the bell balanced and your wrist locked. Gripping too loosely lets the bell tip and fall.
Bottoms-Up Kettlebell Press: Clean the bell to your shoulder and flip it so the base points upward, balanced on your gripping hand. Press it overhead keeping the wrist locked and the bell steady, then lower to the shoulder. Gripping too loosely tips it over.
Double Kettlebell Clean: Stand with a bell in each hand between your feet, hips hinged and back flat. Pull both bells up and rotate your wrists to catch them at your shoulders. Letting the bells crash hard against your wrists means the turnover needs to be softer.
Double Kettlebell Press: Stand with a bell in each hand racked at your shoulders, elbows tucked in. Press both bells overhead until your arms lock out, then lower back to the rack together. Letting one arm lead the other throws off your balance.
Double Kettlebell Swing: Stand with a bell in each hand, hike them back between your legs with a flat back. Drive your hips forward to swing both bells to chest height, then let them swing back down. Squatting the weight up instead of hinging loses glute power.
Get-Up to Elbow: Lie on your back holding a bell overhead in one hand, opposite knee bent and foot flat. Roll onto your propping elbow keeping the kettlebell arm locked and vertical, then reverse back down. Eyes drifting off the bell is the fault.
Gorilla Row: Stand over two bells with feet wide, hips hinged and back flat. Row one bell up towards your ribs while the other hand stays planted on its handle for support, then swap sides. Rounding the back to reach further is the common fault.
Half-Kneeling Kettlebell Press: Kneel with one knee down, the same-side hand holding the bell racked at your shoulder. Press it straight overhead until your arm locks out, then lower back to the shoulder. Leaning sideways to help takes stability off the core.
Kettlebell Around-the-World: Stand tall holding the bell in one hand at hip height. Pass it around your waist from hand to hand, keeping your core braced and posture upright. Letting the bell pull your torso off centre is the main fault.
Kettlebell Bent Press: Stand with the bell racked at your shoulder. Press it up while bending your torso sideways underneath, keeping the arm locked as your hips shift away, then return to standing. Rushing the press before full lock out is the common breakdown.
Kettlebell Clean: Stand with the bell between your feet, hips hinged and back flat. Pull it up close to your body and rotate your wrist to catch it at your shoulder. Letting the bell swing out and away from the body makes the catch hit harder.
Kettlebell Clean and Jerk: Clean the bell to the rack position, then dip your knees and drive it overhead, dropping slightly under it to lock out. Stand tall to finish, then lower back to the rack. Pressing with the arm alone instead of the legs makes it far harder.
Kettlebell Dead Clean: Set the bell on the floor between your feet, hips hinged and back flat, starting each rep from a dead stop. Pull it up and rotate your wrist to catch it at your shoulder. Resetting your posture between reps keeps the pull consistent.
Kettlebell Deadlift: Stand with the bell between your feet, hips hinged back, shins close to vertical. Grip the handle and drive through your heels to stand tall, keeping the bell close to your body. Letting the bell drift forward rounds the lower back.
Kettlebell Double Snatch: Stand with a bell in each hand, hike them back between your legs with a flat back. Drive your hips forward hard to send both bells up, punching your hands through to catch them locked out overhead. One arm lagging throws off balance.
Kettlebell Farmer's Carry: Stand tall holding a bell in each hand at your sides, shoulders pulled back and down. Walk forward with even steps, keeping your torso upright and the bells still. Letting the shoulders round forward under load is the main fault.
Kettlebell Floor Press: Lie on your back with knees bent, a bell held above your shoulder with your upper arm resting on the floor. Press it straight up until your arm locks out, then lower until your elbow lightly touches down. Flaring the elbow shifts the load.
Kettlebell Floor Press (Alternating): Lie on your back with knees bent, a bell in each hand at shoulder height, upper arms resting on the floor. Press one bell up while the other stays down, then swap, torso staying still. Letting the hips twist takes stability off the core.
Kettlebell Floor Press (Single-Arm): Lie on your back with knees bent, one bell held at shoulder height with your upper arm on the floor, other arm by your side. Press the bell up until your arm locks out, then lower with control. Hips rotating towards the arm is the fault.
Kettlebell Forward Lunge (Rack Position): Stand tall with a bell racked at one shoulder. Step forward into a lunge, bending both knees until your back knee nears the floor, then push back to standing. Letting the front knee cave inward is the main fault.
Kettlebell Front Rack Squat (Double): Stand with a bell racked at each shoulder, elbows tucked in close to your ribs. Sit your hips back and down into a squat, torso upright, then drive back up. Letting the elbows drop away from your body pulls your torso forward.
Kettlebell Front Rack Squat (Single-Arm): Stand with one bell racked at your shoulder, elbow tucked in. Sit your hips back and down into a squat, resisting the pull of the bell to one side, then drive back up. Leaning towards the loaded side is the main fault.
Kettlebell Goblet Squat: Hold the bell by the horns close to your chest, feet shoulder-width apart. Sit your hips back and down into a squat, chest tall, elbows inside your knees, then drive back up. Letting the bell pull your shoulders forward rounds the back.
Kettlebell Halo: Hold the bell by the horns at chest height. Circle it around your head, passing close to your skull, core braced and posture tall. Arching the lower back as the bell passes behind your head is the common fault.
Kettlebell Hang Clean: Stand holding the bell at knee height, hips hinged and back flat. Drive your hips forward to pull it up and rotate your wrist to catch it at your shoulder. Letting the bell swing away from the body makes the catch land harder.
Kettlebell Hang Clean (Double, Alternati: Stand holding a bell in each hand at knee height, hips hinged and back flat. Drive your hips forward to pull both bells up, catching one at the shoulder while the other returns, then alternate. Bells swinging wide is the fault.
Kettlebell High Pull: Stand with the bell hanging between your feet, hips hinged and back flat. Drive your hips forward and pull it up close to your body, leading with the elbow, to chest height. Letting the bell swing away turns the pull into a swing.
Kettlebell Jerk: Stand with the bell racked at your shoulder. Dip your knees quickly then drive up, punching the bell overhead as you dip slightly underneath to lock out, then stand tall. Pressing with the arm alone makes the lift far harder.
Kettlebell Jerk (Double): Stand with a bell racked at each shoulder. Dip your knees quickly then drive up, punching both bells overhead as you dip slightly underneath to lock out, then stand tall. One arm locking out before the other throws off balance.
Kettlebell Overhead Carry: Press the bell overhead until your arm locks out, shoulder pulled down away from your ear. Walk forward keeping the bell directly above your shoulder. Letting the arm drift forward of the shoulder puts strain in the wrong place.
Kettlebell Overhead Lunge: Press the bell overhead until your arm locks out. Step forward into a lunge, keeping the bell directly above your shoulder throughout, then push back to standing. Letting the arm lean away from vertical is the main fault.
Kettlebell Overhead Squat: Press the bell overhead until your arm locks out, shoulder pulled down and back. Sit your hips back and down into a squat keeping the bell stacked above your shoulder, then drive back up. The arm drifting forward is the common fault.
Kettlebell Pistol Squat: Hold the bell at your chest or extended in front for counterbalance, standing on one leg. Bend the standing knee into a single-leg squat, then drive back up. Letting the knee cave inward under the extra load is the main fault.
Kettlebell Press (Single-Arm): Stand with the bell racked at one shoulder, elbow tucked in. Press it straight overhead until your arm locks out, then lower back to the rack. Leaning sideways to help the press takes stability off the core.
Kettlebell Push Press: Stand with the bell racked at your shoulder. Dip your knees slightly then drive upward, using the leg drive to help press the bell overhead until it locks out. Pressing with the arm before the legs finish driving loses power.
Kettlebell Rack Carry: Clean the bell to your shoulder, elbow tucked in and wrist straight. Walk forward keeping your torso upright and the bell steady against your chest. Letting the elbow drift away lets the bell pull your posture off centre.
Kettlebell Renegade Row: Hold two bells in a push-up position, hands gripping the handles, feet set wide for stability. Row one bell towards your ribs while balancing on the other hand, then swap sides. Hips rotating towards the rowing side is the common fault.
Kettlebell Reverse Lunge (Rack Position): Stand tall with a bell racked at one shoulder. Step backward into a lunge, bending both knees until your back knee nears the floor, then push through your front foot to stand. The front knee drifting inward is the main fault.
Kettlebell Row (Single-Arm): Hinge forward with a flat back, holding the bell in one hand and the other braced on a bench or your knee. Pull it up towards your ribs, then lower under control. Rotating the torso to help takes tension off the back.
Kettlebell Single-Leg Deadlift: Hold the bell in one hand, standing on the opposite leg. Hinge forward at the hip while your free leg extends back for balance, lowering the bell towards the floor, then return to standing. Hips rotating open signals losing balance.
Kettlebell Suitcase Carry: Stand tall holding one bell at your side like a suitcase, shoulders level. Walk forward with even steps, resisting the pull of the bell to one side. Leaning towards the loaded side is the main fault.
Kettlebell Sumo Deadlift: Stand with feet wide and toes turned out, the bell on the floor between your feet. Push your hips back and grip the bell, then drive through your heels to stand tall. Knees caving inward on the way up is the common fault.
Kettlebell Sumo Deadlift High Pull: Stand with feet wide and toes turned out, the bell between your feet. Deadlift it up, then keep pulling it close to your body to chest height, leading with the elbows. Letting the bell swing away turns the pull into a swing.
Kettlebell Swing (Alternating): Hike the bell back between your legs with a flat back and hinged hips. Drive your hips forward to swing it to chest height, passing it from one hand to the other at the top, then let it swing back down. Squatting it up loses glute power.
Kettlebell Swing (Single-Arm): Hike the bell back between your legs with a flat back and hinged hips, gripping with one hand. Drive your hips forward to swing it to chest height, then let it swing back down. Twisting to counter the single arm is the main fault.
Kettlebell Thruster (Double): Stand with a bell racked at each shoulder. Sit your hips back and down into a squat, then drive up explosively and press both bells overhead as your legs straighten. Pausing between the squat and press loses most of the drive.
Kettlebell Windmill (High): Press the bell overhead until your arm locks out, feet turned slightly away from that side. Keeping the arm vertical, hinge your hips and reach your free hand towards the floor, then return. The overhead arm drifting forward is the fault.
Kettlebell Windmill (Low): Hold the bell racked at your shoulder, not overhead, feet turned slightly away from that side. Hinge your hips and reach your free hand towards the floor while the racked arm stays steady, then return. Rushing the hinge is the fault.
Mixed Kettlebell Carry: Hold one bell racked at your shoulder and the other hanging at your side, opposite hands. Walk forward keeping your torso upright, resisting the pull to either side. Leaning towards the hanging bell is the main fault.
Seated Kettlebell Press: Sit tall on a bench with the bell racked at your shoulder, feet flat on the floor. Press it straight overhead until your arm locks out, then lower back to the rack. Arching away from the bench for height takes work off the shoulder.
See-Saw Kettlebell Press: Stand with a bell racked at each shoulder. Press one overhead while the other stays racked, then lower it as you press the other up, alternating in a steady rhythm. Letting the racked side sag while pressing is the common fault.
Turkish Get-Up (Half): Lie on your back holding a bell overhead in one hand, opposite knee bent, foot flat. Push up through that foot and hand onto your propping arm, bell staying locked overhead, then reverse down. Losing eye contact with the bell is the fault.
Half-Kneeling Landmine Press: Kneel with one knee down, holding the landmine end at your shoulder with the same-side hand. Press the bar up and slightly forward along its arc until your arm locks out, then lower back. Leaning sideways takes stability off the core.
Landmine Anti-Rotation Press (Half-Kneel: Kneel with one knee down, the landmine end held with both hands at your chest. Press the bar straight out without letting your torso rotate towards it, then pull back to your chest. Letting the hips or shoulders twist is what it resists.
Landmine Chest-Supported Row: Lie chest down on an incline bench with the landmine bar passing beneath you, holding the end with both hands. Pull it up towards your chest, squeezing your shoulder blades, then lower under control. A raised chest loses tension.
Landmine Clean: Stand over the landmine bar, feet shoulder-width apart, hips hinged, gripping the end with both hands. Pull it up close to your body and rotate your wrists to catch it at your shoulders. A wide swing makes the catch land harder.
Landmine Floor Press: Lie on your back with knees bent, the landmine end at your shoulder, upper arm resting on the floor. Press it up and forward along its arc until locked out, then lower until your elbow lightly touches down. Drifting wide shifts the load.
Landmine Hack Squat: Face away from the landmine, holding the end between your legs with both hands, bar resting against your shoulders or held low. Sit your hips back and down into a squat, torso upright, then drive back up. Heels lifting is the fault.
Landmine Meadows Row: Stand side on to the landmine bar, hips hinged and back flat, gripping the end with one hand. Pull it up towards your hip along its natural arc, then lower under control. Rounding the back to reach further is the common fault.
Landmine Reverse Lunge: Hold the landmine end at your shoulder or chest with both hands. Step backward into a lunge, bending both knees until your back knee nears the floor, then push through your front foot to stand. The front knee drifting inward is the fault.
Landmine Shrug: Stand over the landmine bar holding the end with both hands at hip height, arms straight. Shrug your shoulders straight up towards your ears, then lower with control. Bending the elbows to help turns the shrug into a row.
Landmine Split Squat: Set your feet in a staggered stance, landmine end held at your shoulder or chest. Lower your back knee towards the floor by bending both knees, then drive through your front foot to stand. A front knee past the toes shifts balance.
Landmine Sumo Squat: Stand with feet wide and toes turned out, holding the landmine end with both hands between your legs. Sit your hips back and down into a squat, chest tall, then drive back up. Knees caving inward on the way up is the common fault.
Landmine Thruster: Hold the landmine end at your shoulders with both hands. Sit your hips back and down into a squat, then drive up explosively and press the bar forward and up as your legs straighten. Pausing between squat and press loses drive.
Landmine Zercher Squat: Cradle the landmine end in the crooks of your elbows, hands together at your chest. Sit your hips back and down into a squat, torso upright, then drive back up. Elbows dropping and the bar sliding down your forearms is the common fault.
Rotational Landmine Press: Stand side on to the landmine, the end held at your chest with both hands. Press the bar out and across your body while rotating through your torso and hips together, then return. Moving only your arms takes power away from the exercise.
Medicine Ball Chest Pass: Hold the ball at your chest, elbows bent, facing a wall or partner. Extend your arms explosively to throw it straight out, then catch it as it returns and absorb it back to your chest. Pushing only with the arms loses most of the power.
Medicine Ball Overhead Throw: Hold the ball overhead with arms extended, feet slightly staggered. Snap your torso forward and throw the ball down and forward into the floor or a wall with full effort. Throwing only with the arms loses most of the power.
Medicine Ball Rotational Throw: Stand side on to a wall holding the ball at your hip with both hands. Rotate your hips and torso together and release the ball explosively towards the wall, then catch the rebound and reset. Arms alone take power off the throw.
Medicine Ball Scoop Toss: Stand with the ball held low near one hip, knees bent. Drive up through your legs and swing the ball diagonally across your body, releasing it up and out at the top. Using only the arms loses most of the power.
Medicine Ball Slam: Hold the ball overhead with arms extended, feet shoulder-width apart. Slam it down into the floor as hard as you can by driving through your torso, then catch the bounce or pick it back up. Slamming with only the arms loses power.
Sled Lateral Drag: Stand side on to the sled with the strap or rope attached, athletic stance with knees bent. Step sideways to drag the sled across the floor, keeping your hips low and chest up throughout. Standing too upright takes tension off the legs.
Sled Reverse Drag: Face the sled and hold the strap with both hands, athletic stance with knees bent. Walk backward to drag the sled towards you, taking controlled steps and keeping tension on the strap. Letting the strap go slack loses the constant tension.
Sled Row: Face away from the sled attached by a strap or rope, in a split or athletic stance. Pull the handles towards your ribs, then extend your arms forward to let the sled slide back before pulling again. Walking the pull loses back tension.
Sandbag Bear-Hug Squat: Hug the sandbag tightly against your chest with both arms wrapped around it. Sit your hips back and down into a squat, chest tall, then drive back up. Letting the bag slide down your chest as you fatigue is the common fault.
Sandbag Bent-Over Row: Hinge forward with a flat back, gripping the sandbag handles or the bag itself in front of your shins. Pull the bag up towards your torso, then lower under control. Rounding the back to lift it off the floor is the main fault.
Sandbag Clean: Stand over the sandbag, feet shoulder-width apart, hips hinged, gripping the bag. Pull it up explosively and catch it against your chest or shoulders, absorbing the weight with bent knees. Catching with straight legs sends impact upward.
Sandbag Front Carry: Hug the sandbag against your chest with both arms wrapped around it, shoulders pulled back and down. Walk forward with even steps, keeping your torso upright. The bag pulling your shoulders forward is the main thing to correct.
Sandbag Get-Up: Lie on your back with the sandbag held against your chest. Roll to one side and use that arm to push yourself up through kneeling to standing, keeping the bag close throughout. Letting the bag swing away makes the transitions harder.
Sandbag Lunge (Bear Hug): Hug the sandbag tightly against your chest. Step forward into a lunge, bending both knees until your back knee nears the floor, then push back to standing. Letting the bag pull your torso forward and down is the common fault.
Sandbag Shouldering: Stand over the sandbag, feet shoulder-width apart, hips hinged. Pull it up explosively and rotate it onto one shoulder in one motion, catching it with bent knees to absorb the weight. Catching with straight legs sends impact into your back.
Sandbag Zercher Carry: Cradle the sandbag in the crooks of your elbows, hands together at your chest. Walk forward with even steps, keeping your torso upright and the bag pulled in close. The bag riding low and pulling your shoulders down is the common fault.
